content.title: About
content.content: Pistachio nuts are the edible seeds of the pistachio tree (Pistacia vera), native to Central Asia and the Middle East, now cultivated in many warm regions worldwide. They have a mildly sweet, buttery flavor and a crunchy texture. Pistachios are eaten raw, roasted, salted or sweetened, and are used in pastries, desserts, spreads, and ice cream.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pistachios belong to the Anacardiaceae family, which also includes cashews and mangoes.
The fruit splits open at maturity, revealing two edible kernels inside.
In ancient Persia, pistachios were a symbol of hospitality and featured in ceremonial feasts.
There are two main commercial varieties: “Kerman” (soft) and “Kara” (hard), differing in taste and texture.
The green color of pistachio kernels can range from pale to bright depending on variety and growing conditions.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Pistachios provide about 20 % protein, making them a good plant‑based protein source.

items.title: Heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: Most of the fat in pistachios is monounsaturated, which supports cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in amino‑acid metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Lutein, zeaxanthin and polyphenols in pistachios help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports gut microbiota
items.content: Fiber and prebiotic compounds promote the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Tree‑nut allergy
items.content: Pistachios can trigger allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Because they are high in calories, pistachios should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Added salt and flavorings
items.content: Salted or flavored pistachios contain extra sodium and additives, which may be undesirable for people with hypertension.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Pistachios contain oxalates, so those prone to kidney stones should limit intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pistachios can be enjoyed as a snack, tossed into salads, yogurts, oatmeal, baked goods, or processed into pistachio butter and pistachio‑crusted dishes. They are often sold salted, but unsalted versions are available. Soaking softens them and may aid digestion.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pistachios in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent oil oxidation. Discard nuts that smell rancid or have a stale taste.
